panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (a, b). a: Panel (a is a clinical photo of a child presenting with facial dysmorphisms (prominent forehead, broad nasal root, hypertelorism) and features consistent with abdominal distention and short stature, supporting the diagnosis of trichohepatoenteric syndrome as per the caption and in-text. b: Panel b is a clinical photo of a child presenting with facial dysmorphisms (prominent forehead, broad nasal root, hypertelorism) and features consistent with abdominal distention and short stature, supporting the diagnosis of trichohepatoenteric syndrome as per the caption and in-text.

panels.figure_caption: (a) and (b) Note the prominent forehead and cheeks, hypertelorism and broad nasal root, short stature, and abdominal distention of the child.
in_text_mentions: was hospitalized several times for workup of failure to thrive. As seen in the attached photo facial dysmorphism (prominent forehead, broad based nasal bridge, and hypertelorism) is evident (Figures 1(a) and 1(b)). Hair changes such as woolly and easily removable hair and light coloration were evident in our case. Two other children in the family (his cousin a one-year-old girl weighing 7 Kg with developmental delay and another cousin a 9-year-old boy weighing 16 Kg) also showed somewhat similar symptoms (Figures 2 and 3). panels.rationale: The image is a microscopic view of a hair shaft from a child, showing kinking, which is a manifestation of trichohepatoenteric syndrome (specifically related to woolly brittle hair) reported in the figure's caption and article text.

panels.figure_caption: Hair shaft of the child showing kinking.
in_text_mentions: Microscopic examination of hair shafts of the first case revealed aniso- and poikilotrichosis with kinking and breakage but no typical trichorrhexis nodosa was seen (Figure 5).
